name: Don Bradman
one_line: Career Test batting average 99.94; no completed career in Test history has reached 62.

facts.claim: career Test batting average of 99.94 - 6,996 runs and 29 centuries in 52 Tests
facts.note: Wikipedia: 'considered by some to be the greatest achievement by any sportsman in any major sport.'

facts.claim: a batting average is runs scored divided by times out; above 50 is considered the benchmark of a great batsman
facts.note: Wikipedia verbatim: 'A batting average of above 50 is considered by many as a benchmark to distinguish between a good and a great batsman.' The explainer that makes 99.94 legible to non-cricket viewers.

facts.claim: the next-best COMPLETED career average in all of Test history is 61.87 (Adam Voges, retired 2017, min 20 innings)
facts.note: TRAP DEFUSED: an active player (Kamindu Mendis, ~62.66 as of 2026) may rank above Voges on some cuts, so never say '61.87 is second best' flatly - say 'no completed career has done better than 61.87' or 'nobody who finished a career got past 62'. Voges framing sourced at his retirement: 'best average since Bradman'.

facts.claim: in his final innings, at The Oval on 14 August 1948, he needed four runs to retire with an average of exactly 100 - England gave him three cheers, and he was bowled second ball for nought by Eric Hollies
facts.note: THE closer. Average fell from 101.39 to 99.94. Australia won by an innings, so he never batted again. Most famous duck in cricket history. Reported speech only - no quotes.

facts.claim: as a boy in Bowral he practiced alone with a cricket stump and a golf ball, hitting rebounds off a curved water tank stand
facts.note: Origin beat. Wikipedia: 'the ball rebounded at high speed and varying angles.' A stump is far narrower than a bat; a golf ball far smaller than a cricket ball.

facts.claim: scored 974 runs in the 1930 Ashes series - still the record for any Test series, unmatched as of 2022
facts.note: Wikipedia: 'no-one has matched or exceeded 974 runs or three double centuries in one Test series.' At an average of 139.14 in that series.

facts.claim: England devised an entirely new bowling tactic - Bodyline, 1932-33 - specifically to curb him; he still averaged 56.57 in that series
facts.note: Wikipedia: devised to 'curb his almost uncanny skill'; 56.57 was 'just 57% of his career mean' - and would still rank among the best careers ever. A whole strategy, and a diplomatic crisis, engineered against one man.

facts.claim: statistician Charles Davis rated Bradman 4.4 standard deviations above the mean; for Michael Jordan to dominate basketball equally he would have needed a career average of 43 points per game - Jordan retired at 30.1
facts.note: From Davis's statistical study, widely reproduced. Attribute in script ('one statistician did the math'). Jordan career scoring average 30.12 - say 'retired at 30' or 'just over 30'.

facts.claim: the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's post office box in every capital city is 9994, chosen in Bradman's honour
facts.note: Requested by ABC GM Charles Moses, a personal friend; in effect since 1983. Authenticated by ABC staff and 'The A-Z of Bradman' - not urban legend. THE closer.

facts.claim: Bodyline was fast bowling aimed at the batsman's body, expecting a defensive deflection to be caught; devised for the 1932-33 Ashes specifically to neutralize Bradman
Bodyline escalated into a diplomatic incident between the British and Australian governments - Australia's PM warned of trade consequences
facts.note: Wikipedia: 'escalated into a diplomatic incident'; PM Joseph Lyons warned of 'severe economic hardships' from British boycotts.

facts.claim: in 1935 the MCC changed the Laws of cricket: 'direct attack' bowling was declared unfair and umpires empowered to stop it
facts.note: The sport literally rewrote its laws because of tactics invented against one man.

comparison.second_label: the best anyone else finished with
comparison.gap_description: 99.94 against 61.87 - the biggest gap between first and second in any major sport.

story_beat: In his last innings he needed four runs to end with an average of exactly 100. The England players gave him three cheers as he arrived - and two balls later he was walking back, bowled for nought. His team won by an innings, so the chance never came again: 99.94, forever.
